title_en: On the Saying, “The Lord Created Me”
author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: Eustathius defends the full divinity of the Word against those who interpreted Proverbs 8:22 (“The Lord created me”) as applying to the divine Son, and he recounts the maneuvers of Eusebius’ party at the Council of Nicaea.
argument: Eustathius argues that the Word, being God from eternity with the Father, was not created and did not become from a woman; rather, the man whom the Word fashioned and wore is the one born of the Virgin, placed under the law, crucified, and raised. He distinguishes the impassible divine Spirit of Christ from the passible human temple, so that suffering and weakness belong to the man, not to the Godhead. He supports this from the Gospels, Paul, and the apostles’ preaching that God made the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ. Finally, he recalls how at Nicaea the letter of Eusebius was exposed as blasphemy, the Arians anathematized the condemned doctrine under pressure, and then secretly continued to promote it.

outline.move: The Word is eternal God and creator, while the man formed in the Virgin’s womb is the temple the Word wore; the Son is the Father’s image, and the man is the image of the Son.

The man born of the Virgin was circumcised and offered purifications under the law, not because the Word needed them, but to redeem those under the law’s curse; the risen man, not the Word who comes from heaven and dwells in the Father’s bosom, says to Mary that he has not yet ascended to the Father, reserving the firstfruits of his departure, and the crucified man is the one God made Lord and Christ.

The incorporeal divine Spirit cannot suffer, be crucified, die, or be buried; the man suffered and died, while the divine Spirit remained impassible and active everywhere, and weakness must be attributed to the man, not to the fullness of deity.

The divine Wisdom is not contained or defiled by the body’s suffering, any more than the sun is altered by the many outrages it endures everywhere on earth; Eustathius then recounts the exposure of Eusebius’ blasphemous letter at Nicaea and the Arians’ deceptive condemnation of their own doctrine.

cast.name: Eustathius
cast.who: Bishop of Antioch and the author, defending Nicene orthodoxy against Arian interpretations.

cast.name: Eusebius
cast.who: Leader of the party whose written statement was exposed as blasphemous at Nicaea.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: Apostle cited for the distinction between the Son and the image of the Son, and for the crucified Lord of glory.

cast.name: Luke
cast.who: Evangelist cited for the circumcision and presentation of the child Jesus.

cast.name: Mary
cast.who: The woman who wished to touch the risen Jesus and was told he had not yet ascended.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: Prophet cited for the final defeat of the ungodly.

scripture: The author cites the Gospels and Pauline epistles by traditional names (Luke, Philippians) and refers to the law’s provisions for purification and firstborn offerings. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where applicable; modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and LXX Psalm numbering where the author’s usage reflects it.
uncertain: The exact date of composition beyond early 4th century
The precise number of bishops at Nicaea, which Eustathius himself says he cannot state with certainty
Whether the work originally had a named addressee

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-open: λύσατε τὸν ναὸν τοῦτον, καὶ ἐν τρισὶν ἡμέραις ἐγερῶ αὐτόν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Jesus is quoted in u01-open and u01-rem-early, but NOT in u01-rem-mid. The u01-rem-mid section contains no direct quotation from Jesus; it discusses his power over his soul (John 10:18) but as paraphrase, not direct speech marked by ἐκφωνεῖ or φάσκων.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-early: Κύριον αὐτὸν καὶ Χριστὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε, τοῦτον τὸν Ἰησοῦν, ὃν ὑμεῖς ἐσταυρώσατε
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is quoted in u01-open, but the quotation in u01-rem-early is from the apostles (Peter in Acts), not Paul. The brief misattributes the quotation "Κύριον αὐτὸν καὶ Χριστὸν ὁ θεὸς ἐποίησε" to Paul when the source introduces it with "καθάπερ οἱ ἀπόστολοι...φασιν" (as the apostles say).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul ... "for the crucified Lord of glory"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-mid: Εἰ γὰρ ὁ Παῦλος ἔφρασε τὸν Κύριον τῆς δόξης ἐσταυρῶσθαι
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is cited in u01-rem-mid for "the Lord of glory crucified," but this is Eustathius's report of what Paul said, not a direct quotation of Paul in the source. The actual direct quotation of Paul in u01-open is about "συμμόρφους τῆς εἰκόνος τοῦ Υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ" (conformed to the image of his Son). The brief should clarify that "Lord of glory crucified" is Eustathius's paraphrase of Paul's meaning, not a direct citation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Isaiah ... "Prophet cited for the final defeat of the ungodly"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-close: πάλιν ἡττηθήσονται κατὰ τὸν σεμνόφωνον προφήτην Ἡσαΐαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Isaiah is mentioned as "the solemn-voiced prophet" but no specific prophecy is quoted or identified; Eustathius only alludes generally to Isaiah's testimony about defeat of the ungodly without citing specific words. The brief should note this is an allusion, not a citation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He supports this from the Gospels, Paul, and the apostles' preaching that God made the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-early: καθάπερ οἱ ἀπόστολοι τῷ αἰσθητῷ Ἰσραὴλ ὁμοφρόνως διαλεγόμενοί φασιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The preaching that "God made the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ" is attributed to "the apostles" (specifically Peter's speech in Acts), not to Paul. The brief conflates Paul with the apostles on this point.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close move: "The divine Wisdom is not contained or defiled by the body's suffering, any more than the sun is altered by the many outrages it endures everywhere on earth"
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: u01-rem-close: Οὐ γὰρ εἴσω τῶν σωματικῶν ὄγκων ἡ ἀνωτάτω Σοφία καθειργμένη περιέχεται... Ἀλλὰ θεία τις οὖσα... 31 Εἰ δ' ὁ ἥλιος...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The sun analogy appears in section 31, which is part of u01-rem-close, but the brief's summary conflates two distinct arguments: (a) Wisdom is not contained in bodily masses like liquid in vessels (section before 31), and (b) the sun analogy (section 31). More importantly, the sun "endures outrages" (ὑπομένων αἰκίας) without being changed—this is the analogy, but the brief's phrasing "outrages it endures" could mislead. The Greek says the sun undergoes/undergoes outrages (passive), not actively endures them.
